Unit 1 of 10: Meaning of Accounting; Accounting as a Source of Information

Key ideas

  • Accounting (AICPA, 1941): "the art of recording, classifying and summarising in a significant manner and in terms of money, transactions and events which are, in part at least, of a financial character, and interpreting the results thereof."
  • Modern view (AAA, 1966): identifying, measuring and communicating economic information to permit informed judgements and decisions by users.
  • Attributes: economic events; identification, measurement, recording and communication; interested users.
  • Process: identifying → measuring → recording (journal) → classifying (ledger) → summarising (trial balance, financial statements) → analysing and interpreting → communicating.
  • Book-keeping is the recording part (routine, clerical); accounting is wider — it includes summarising, analysing and interpreting.
  • Accounting is an information system: it collects data, processes it and communicates information to users.

Worked examples

Example 1: Is the death of the firm's best salesperson recorded in the books? Answer: No — it cannot be measured in money (only financial events are recorded).

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) Recording of transactions in the books of original entry is called: (a) classifying (b) recording (c) summarising (d) interpreting. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) Name the stage where transactions are grouped in the ledger. Answer: classifying.
  3. (2 marks) Distinguish between book-keeping and accounting. Answer: book-keeping — recording and classifying; routine and clerical (1); accounting — also summarises, analyses and interprets; needs judgement (1).
  4. (3 marks) Explain three attributes of accounting from its definition. Answer: concerned with economic events of an organisation (1); involves identifying, measuring, recording and communicating (1); serves interested users (1).
  5. (3 marks) Why is accounting called an information system? Answer: it collects data on transactions (input) (1); processes them through journal, ledger and statements (1); communicates useful information to users (output) (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Recording non-monetary events. 2. Book-keeping = accounting. 3. Stages out of order. 4. Missing communication. 5. Definitions without key words.

Quick recall

  1. Grouping in ledger? 2. Summarising produces? 3. Book-keeping ends at? 4. Non-financial events recorded? 5. Accounting output?

Answers: 1) Classifying. 2) Trial balance, financial statements. 3) Recording/classifying. 4) No. 5) Information for users.
